rationale: D-29 targets the small-distance half of the problem, which the verified high-distance F_8 bounds do not. C-19 already records additive quaternary codes that beat every F_4-linear code of the same length and cardinality, but only at large distance and dimension 4. Here the linear obstruction is the Edel–Bierbrauer theorem that PG(4,4) has no 42-cap, so no F_4-linear [42,37,4] code exists, while an additive code is only a set of 42 binary 2-flats in F_2^{10} whose triples span dimension 6. That is a real gap an explicit matrix can fill, and a hit would be a finite object whose size and distance are machine-checkable. The first milestone is small and falsifiable: the six secants through P=(0,1,1,0,1) give 64 deletion sets, each with an exhaustive insertion search and either a rank-checked H or a negative count. The stop criterion is equally sharp and does not treat a timeout as nonexistence. The neighborhood of one seed cannot decide the general existence question, but it is a sound, concrete pilot rather than a restatement of the known large-distance separations.

The reversal mechanism is real, but D-3 is not worth pursuing as stated. Its idea and four-cell milestone are identical to D-20, so it is not a new direction. C-24, written for this same search, shows that choosing the orientation by aggregate prefix/suffix scores can raise the worst overlap; the exact objective must be used, and nothing in the proposal exploits the autocorrelation invariance beyond random trials. The stop threshold is also obsolete: C-9 records published upper bounds already below 0.38086, while D-3 abandons the search only if 10,000 trials fail to beat 0.390. A construction at 0.389 would not improve the Erdős constant. The four-cell identity only shows that a reversal can move the overlap, which the milestone text already computes, and does not justify a large search aimed below a superseded cutoff.

D-20 copies D-3 verbatim: the same factor-reversal idea, the same four-cell milestone, and the same 0.390 stop threshold. It is not a new direction. D-3 already has a verified result, C-24, showing that minimizing aggregate boundary scores over orientations can increase the worst overlap, so the proposed search has no orientation rule that is known to help. C-9 records published upper bounds already below 0.38086, so a search that only demands a value below 0.390 cannot improve the Erdős constant even if it meets its own stop complement. The four-cell calculation is a mechanism check already written into the milestone, not a reason to run a duplicate 10,000-trial search.

The chamber LP is mathematically sound and distinct from factor reversal, and C-23 already carried out the first milestone: the 3/5-to-1/2 move and an exact 8-interval optimum of 499/1112, certified in rational arithmetic. That optimum is about 0.449. C-9 records the competitive upper bound below 0.38086, so the milestone does not approach the constant the problem asks to improve. The remaining plan — 50 initializations at 64 and 128 intervals, at most three chamber crossings, success defined as a 10^{-8} drop from the seed — does not start from a record height vector and does not require beating the published bound. Fixed generic heights cannot represent the known step constructions. D-5 is the same proposal again. Further work on this specification is not worth the effort.

D-5 repeats D-4 word for word, including the chamber-LP idea, the 3/5-to-1/2 milestone, and the stop rule of fifty seeds at 64 and 128 intervals. It is not new. C-23 already implemented that milestone for D-4 and certified an 8-interval optimum of 499/1112, about 0.449, which the claim itself says does not improve the unrestricted constant. C-9 records a published upper bound below 0.38086. A duplicate search whose success condition is only a 10^{-8} drop from a generic seed cannot improve that bound and is not worth a second effort.

The H-orbit model is sound, but D-31 is not a new direction. D-30 already asks for the same exact search: all H-orbits of eight-subsets of F_2^4, 1,670 binary variables, 546 coverage constraints, target at most 113 blocks, starting from the verified 114-block design in C-13. C-36 explains why that relaxation is the right one for an odd improvement: an H-invariant 113-block covering must split {H, H xor 8} and cannot be a union of full G-orbits. D-31 repeats that formulation and only shortens the pilot from D-30's 24 CPU-hours to 3,600 CPU-seconds. A shorter duplicate run is not worth a separate effort; any solver attempt should be charged to D-30, and a timeout must still be reported as unresolved rather than as a lower bound on C(16,8,5).

D-30 is the original exact search for an H-invariant (16,8,5) covering with at most 113 blocks, and it is distinct from D-21's incidence-type synthesis. C-13 gives a verified 114-block covering by full F_2^4 translations. Those orbits all have even size, so they cannot total 113. C-36 shows that any H-invariant 113-block covering must instead split the singleton orbit {H, H xor 8} and have translation stabilizer exactly H. The proposed ILP encodes precisely that class: 1,670 free H-orbits, 546 coverage rows, and a budget of 113, with both singleton orbits free so even improvements are not excluded. The instance is small enough that one 24-hour single-core run is worth doing. The milestone is machine-checkable — regenerate the OPB, replay the 114-block control, and return a checked covering, a checked infeasibility certificate, or UNKNOWN — and the stop rule correctly refuses to treat a timeout as a lower bound on unrestricted C(16,8,5). D-31 is only a shorter copy of this same pilot and should not be run separately.

D-21 is a different experiment from the H-orbit search in D-30 and D-31. It starts from the verified 27-block (61,25,3) covering in C-8 and asks whether two new point signatures can raise the point count to 62 while keeping 27 blocks of size 25. The coverage rule is correct: if every triple of signatures, including repetitions, has a common block, then integer multiplicities still cover every triple, and the only extra constraint is block load at most 25. The proposal already shows, by an exact weighting, that no multiplicity change of the original 28 signatures reaches 62 points, and that one exhibited extra signature is also insufficient, so the two-signature search is the indicated next step rather than a repeat of those checks. The milestone is small and falsifiable: a two-hour MILP or SAT run must return blocks plus an exhaustive triple check, a machine-checkable infeasibility certificate, or UNKNOWN. A negative answer is correctly scoped to this restricted family and is still worth having before a broader search.
